title: As one that serveth (Luke 22:24–27)
hook: at the supper they argue about greatness; he says I am among you as one that serves
carry: servant of the servants of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, anamnesis: the bread and the cup in the upper room. Your line was do this. Did you pause before a meal? Day four hundred eighty.

In Luke, the very next thing after the bread and the cup is an argument. Jesus has just said this is my body, given for you. He's just told them one of them will betray him. And the apostles, at that same table, fall to arguing about which of them is the greater. A family bickering over who gets the good chair at a hospital bedside. Mark and Matthew tell of a similar quarrel earlier, on the road; Luke sets it here, at the Last Supper. Today, how Jesus answers it.
screen: `RIGHT AFTER THE BREAD AND CUP.` → `WHICH OF US IS THE GREATER?` → `LUKE SETS IT AT THE SUPPER.`

segments.voice: Luke says: "And there was also a strife amongst them, which of them should seem to be the greater." Jesus doesn't scold them for wanting to matter. He redraws what mattering means. The kings of the nations lord it over people, he says, and the people in power like to be called benefactors. "But you not so." Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves. Then he asks a simple question about the room they're sitting in. Who's greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? At any dinner the answer is plain: the one at table. "But I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." He doesn't say I'm like a servant. He says, I am in the midst of you as one serving. Present tense. Right now, at this table. The Greek word is diakonon, the one who waits on tables, from the same family as the word deacon. The Catholic Church builds this into its own shape. Every priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, a servant, and that service is meant never to wear off. Pope Gregory the Great called himself servant of the servants of God, servus servorum Dei, and popes still use the title at the head of official letters. The pope's own title borrows the job at the bottom of the table. A title doesn't guarantee anyone lives up to it. It names the standard Jesus set at the table, the night before he died: greatness measured by service.
screen: `A STRIFE ABOUT GREATNESS.` · `BUT YOU NOT SO.` · `DIAKONON: THE ONE WHO WAITS TABLES.` · `SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD.` · then, large: `I AM IN THE MIDST OF YOU AS HE THAT SERVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without being asked. Settle, and breathe. Picture the rooms you'll be in today: home, work, a bus, a store. Where is there a small job nobody wants? Dishes in the sink, a full trash bag, a spill, a coworker drowning in a task, a parent who's tired. Choose one, and decide to just do it without announcing it or waiting to be thanked. Picture yourself doing it quietly. If you pray, offer it as service. The bell holds the time.
Diakonon. The Greek word behind serveth: the one who waits on tables, Jesus' answer to his apostles' argument at the Last Supper. Today's word.
Your line: servant of the servants of God. Today, do one small job nobody asked you to do, and don't mention it. Day four hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Every Catholic priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, and the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper provides for the priest to wash the feet of members of the congregation, in memory of Christ serving at the Last Supper.

original.note: Greek: the one serving, waiting on tables. The root of the word deacon.

trapdoor: what you thought: as one that serveth is a nice humble saying.
what it means: at his last meal, Jesus places himself in the lowest job at the table and makes that the measure of greatness.
what a scholar hears: diakonon, the one waiting tables; Gregory the Great's title servus servorum Dei is still used by popes.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut stock lines ('easy to skip, almost painful', 'so human it hurts'); 'only Luke puts it here' now says what Mark and Matthew do (cited Mark 10); paraphrases follow the Douay's 'greater/younger'; cut the uncited 'around the year 600' and '590–604' dates and the 'highest office... lowest job' superlatives; 'root of deacon' softened to 'same family'.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 22:24, 22:26 ('But you not so') and 22:27.
The index carry 'as one that serveth' differs slightly from the Douay 'as he that serveth'; the carry is kept exactly as indexed and the voice quotes the Douay. Owner may wish to align the index.
Servus servorum Dei: used by Gregory the Great (pope 590–604) and by later popes in official documents. Confirm phrasing.
Luke places the dispute at the supper; Mark and Matthew place a similar dispute earlier. Confirm 'only Luke puts this argument right here'.
